She said it lightly, but Gabriel felt the ground tilt slightly under his preparation. His appeal stack, the one defending Schenck, suddenly looked thinner. He had been planning to use the fire line as a shield, the way people did at lunch tables and in comment sections, as if it settled things. Now the shield had a history.

He went back to the pamphlets themselves, the ones Schenck had mailed to draftees, and the doubt began to coagulate into something more solid: not that one side was right, but that the famous line had done a kind of double duty for a century, standing in for an argument while making people forget there had ever been an argument. Ms. Wanjiru had said something on the first day that he'd dismissed as teacherly fog, that the law was less about finding the truth than about deciding who bears a cost. It came back to him now with actual edges.

Lisa arrived with a printed article and the particular expression of someone who has been proven right. "Guess what I found," she said, sliding into the third chair. "Your case is the same as my uncle's citation in his old political science notes. Holmes wrote that line in 1919, Schenck v. United States, and people have been misusing it ever since, like it's some kind of natural law instead of one justice's opinion in one war." She waited for him to be annoyed. He was not, quite.

"I got there already," Gabriel said, and pulled his two stacks together into one. "The problem is it's a good line. It's vivid. If I'm the government I want it, and it's honest to use it, because Holmes actually wrote it, in Schenck itself, in 1919, about this exact kind of case. But if I'm the appeal, I have to stand up and say, the man who gave you that image was deciding whether a pamphleteer goes to prison, and a theatre was never in front of him." He looked at the merged stack, the pages out of order now, government mixed with appeal, and found he could not fully separate them again, and did not want to.

"You could be an egoist about it," Manreet said, swallowing the last segment of orange. "Just argue whichever side wins and stop caring."

"That's not what an egoist is," Lisa said. "An egoist just acts in his own interest. Arguing to win is basically his job."

Gabriel laughed once, quietly, mindful of the room. There was an atavistic pull in all of it, he thought, some old instinct that wanted a tribe and a flag and a side chosen before the thinking started, and the assignment was designed to starve that instinct, or at least to make him notice when it growled. He still did not know which side he would rather argue on Friday. He knew only that he would be honest about the line when he used it, wherever he stood, and that the coin had not yet been flipped.

He began sorting the pages back into two stacks, slowly, deciding which arguments belonged where, and Lisa leaned over and pulled one sheet out of the appeal pile and set it on the government side without a word.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
The bus was fifteen minutes late and Kaitlyn had the folded pages on her knees before the driver had even closed the doors. Ms. Fraser had kept her after class with the assignment: take the chapter from the Victorian novel, the one where the mill owner shows his new visitor around the works, and read it twice, once through a feminist lens and once through a Marxist one. An essay by Friday. Kaitlyn had nodded in the doorway, and only on the stairs did she understand that she did not actually know what a lens was, not in the way Ms. Fraser meant it, not as something you could hold up to a page and see differently through.

Mederic was already in the fourth row, headphones around his neck, a battered copy of the same novel open on his bag. He pulled his feet off the seat when he saw her. "You get the Fraser thing?" he said. "The lenses?"

"I got the pages," Kaitlyn said. "That's what I got."

They read together as the bus lurched out of the lot, and Kaitlyn found she could do the feminist reading almost without thinking. The only woman in the chapter was the owner's daughter, who poured tea and said nothing while the men discussed wages. She was given one paragraph of description, all her wrists and her downcast eyes, and Kaitlyn underlined it so hard the pen went through to the next page. That part was easy. She wrote in the margin, she exists to be looked at, and felt the small heat of being right.

The Marxist part refused to open. She read the scene again and saw men, a mill, smoke, a ledger, and she could not find the argument hiding in it. "Is it about the smoke?" she said. "Is it, like, the conditions?"

"Stephanie said something about it at lunch," Mederic said. "She did the whole thing last night. She was sorting people."

"Sorting them how?"

He shrugged and turned up a palm, and Kaitlyn leaned back against the cold window and hated, briefly, how easily other people seemed to arrive at things.

Stephanie got on two stops later, pink from the wind, and dropped into the seat across the aisle. "You're doing the mill chapter," she said, not a question, because Kaitlyn's face had already said it. "Okay. Do you have a whiteboard?"

"I'm on a bus, Steph."

"Then picture one." Stephanie held up her hand as though wiping it clean. "Two columns. Owners on one side, workers on the other. The guy with the mill, all the land, the machines, the factory itself, that's his column. In Marxist terms the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, the factories and the land. The proletariat owns nothing but its labour and has to sell it for wages. That's your whole second column, everybody in the novel who works for him."

Kaitlyn looked down at the chapter and the sorting happened in her head, quiet and seismic. The owner's daughter, the tea-pourer, went into neither column, and that was where the two lenses touched. The woman owned nothing and worked for no wages; she was traded rather than paid, moved from one man's house to another's like the deed to a field. Kaitlyn wrote a single line in the margin, bridge between the columns, and drew a little arrow, and understood that she was drawing an isthmus between two islands she had thought were separate countries.

"It's not that they cancel out," she said slowly. "It's that the same woman lands in the gap between both readings. She's not an owner and she's not exactly a worker."

"I put her under owners," Stephanie said. "Her father's money covers her."

"Maybe," Kaitlyn said, and was surprised to hear herself defend an uncertainty she'd only just discovered. "But she doesn't own anything. She can't. That might be the point."

The bus went over the crossing by the grain elevator and everybody's pens jumped. Kaitlyn kept writing, faster now, the two columns going up her arm and into the essay she could suddenly see the shape of. She would argue that the daughter was the seam where the readings met, and she would argue it in Ms. Fraser's room on Friday, and she had the whole ride home, and the whole ride after that, to get it down.

"Careful," Mederic said, watching her. "Fraser'll ask you what you'd claim if the daughter inherited the mill. She likes to prognosticate your follow-up question before you've answered the first one."

"Then I'll say I don't know yet," Kaitlyn said. "Honestly."

Stephanie laughed and Mederic shook his head, and outside the window the mill town they never usually looked at went by, the actual factory with its actual fence, and Kaitlyn counted the cars in the lot and then the bicycles stacked by the gate. The bus stopped and three men in the same grey shirts got on, swipe cards first, then row by row toward the back.

She watched them the whole way to the front of her notebook, and then she wrote, "Which column?" and underlined it twice.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
story:
The trail climbed through pines that smelled like rain even though the sky was clear, and Isabella carried the folded graph in her back pocket the whole way up, the way other people carried a map. Mr. Le had assigned it on Thursday: read the curve, find where it began, calculate the rise. On Saturday he had somehow convinced four of them to hike with him anyway, as if the homework would follow them up the mountain.

"The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen," Alex was saying, two switchbacks below her, slightly out of breath. "So how does a tiny fraction of anything matter?"

"Because it's not about how much there is," Yacine said. "It's about what it does."

"Which is what, exactly? In normal words, not Mr. Le's words."

That was the question Isabella had been dreading, because she was supposed to be the one who could answer it. Her mother had spent the week eulogizing her as the science one in the family, telling an aunt on the phone that Isabella could explain anything if you gave her a minute, and now the minute had arrived on a dirt path at ten in the morning and she had nothing prepared. She knew the phrase greenhouse gases. She knew they trapped heat. But between those two sentences lay a gap she could fall into.

"The sun sends light through the air," she said slowly, when the trail leveled and the three of them caught up. "The ground soaks it up and warms up, and then it sends heat back out. Different kind of radiation. And some gases let the light through but catch the heat on the way out. Like a blanket that's clear from one side."

"Like a car in a parking lot," Yacine said.

"A car in a parking lot, yes." She felt something click into place, two ways of saying it that agreed with each other.

Mr. Le, walking behind them the whole time, said nothing, which Isabella had learned to distrust. He did that when there was a hole in what you'd said, and he liked to wait and see whether you'd find it yourself.

They stopped at an outcrop where the valley opened below, the town small and pale in the haze. Alex flopped down and pulled out a granola bar. Isabella took out the graph instead and flattened it on the rock with her water bottle holding down one corner. The line climbed in small jagged steps, rising and rising, and at the bottom left it began at a label she had glanced at Thursday night and then, in her written answer, had gotten wrong. She had written 350. She had not checked. She had been tired, and 350 had looked like the kind of number that started things.

She stared at the axis now, and the axis stared back.

"What," Yacine said.

"Nothing." Her face was hot. The number on the left edge, the very first reading, taken at a place called Mauna Loa in March of 1958, was about 313 parts per million. Not 350. She had turned in the homework already. Friday, before school, into the basket on his desk, and Mr. Le was standing eight feet away eating a handful of trail mix and pretending not to watch her.

She counted the rise instead, to see how bad it was. From 313 to where the line ended, decades of small steepening steps. If she'd started from 350, the whole increase came out wrong, smaller than the truth. She did the subtraction twice, with her finger on the paper, and the second answer matched the first.

"Mr. Le," she said.

"Mm."

"I got the starting value wrong. On the homework. I put 350 and it's 313. The first reading, at Mauna Loa, in March 1958. So the rise I calculated is too small."

He chewed for a moment. "How much too small?"

"Thirty-seven parts per million too small." Saying the number out loud made it worse and better at once, the way confession usually worked. "I didn't read the axis carefully. I was tired."

"You knew before you told me," he said. It wasn't a question.

"I knew just now. From the graph. But I suspected Thursday night and didn't go back and check." Below them the haze thickened, or thinned; she couldn't tell which, and that was the trouble with the whole subject, she thought, that you had to trust instruments because your eyes were no good at noticing a change this slow. Except the instruments kept being right, and people kept being tired.

"You're belligerent when you're wrong, you know that?" Alex said, but she was grinning. "You go all quiet and then you confess like you're turning yourself in."

"It's not confession, it's correction," Yacine said. "In Mr. Le's vernacular."

"Redo it," Mr. Le said. "Monday. Show me both numbers, the one you used and the one you should have used, and tell me which one you trust and why." He shouldered his pack and started up the trail again, and Isabella folded the graph along its old creases, carefully, keeping the axis on the outside.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
story:
The travel agency sat between a nail salon and a shuttered video store, and Eva had walked past it for years without once going in. She went in now because Mr. Henry had told her, at the career fair, that the back room held something more useful than brochures. "People think I sell trips," he had said. "What I actually sell is geography. Come Saturday and I'll show you what that means."

The back room smelled of old paper and toner. Mr. Henry cleared a space on the desk, lifted a stack of pamphlets about cruises nobody took anymore, and exhumed from beneath them a battered laptop. "County released its floodplain data last month," he said. "Nobody's looked at it. Everybody looks at the river when it's already in their living room." He opened a program Eva didn't recognize, a map of the city veined with streets, and showed her how to layer the county's flood zones over the parcels, then the parcels over the tax records. Where the layers crossed, houses she knew turned a color she hadn't expected.

Foster came in at noon with two sandwiches and an agenda of his own. He wanted Mr. Henry to price him a bus route across three states for the summer, before college swallowed him whole. He leaned over Eva's shoulder while he ate, unimpressed. "It's a map," he said. "I have one of those on my phone." Eva shaded the floodplain blue and the housing values amber, and where the two overlaid, the east side of the river went green. "That green," she said, "is cheap houses inside the hundred-year zone. My phone doesn't do that."

She had come with a reason, though she hadn't told anyone what it was yet. A family friend was closing on a house near the river at the end of the month, and her mother had said, over dinner, that it was a steal, that the street never flooded, that people there had lived dry for years. Eva zoomed until the parcel took shape. It sat inside the blue.

"Mr. Henry," she said carefully, "what does one percent actually mean. The yearly chance." He rocked back in his chair. "One percent a year. That's what the zone says." She pulled the calculator toward her and worked it through, and the answer she got was not the answer she had assumed. "One percent every year, over thirty years of a mortgage," she said. "That comes out to about a twenty-six percent chance it floods at least once. That's more than one in four." Foster stopped chewing. "Twenty-six," he said. "That's basically a coin flip with better odds for the water."

Mr. Henry was quiet for a moment, and Eva noticed that he had gone still in a way she hadn't seen in him before. "Whose house?" he asked. And here was the thing she had been carrying all morning and had not said aloud: the house on the river was his. He was retiring there in June, closing the agency whose customer lists had thinned year by year, attrition he never mentioned but clearly felt, and the woman buying his building had already signed. He had called it his steal.

"You've been on that lot since March," Eva said. "You never thought to run your own data?" He laughed, but not much reached his eyes. "I sell other people's futures. I didn't think to price my own." He looked at the green shading a long time. Eva saved the file twice, then a third time, to a drive and to the cloud, because it seemed suddenly like the kind of thing that shouldn't exist in only one place.

Foster, who had wanted a bus route and gotten a geography lesson, had changed his mind about something while they talked. He asked Mr. Henry to pull the route up anyway, but he kept glancing at the screen. "Before I blow my savings crossing three states," he said, "maybe check whether those highways like rivers." He pointed at the map, and Eva saw he was already reading it the new way, tracing roads that hugged the blue.

Mr. Henry picked up the phone and dialed a number he clearly knew by heart. He turned away from them toward the window with its faded posters of beaches. "It's me," he said. "About the house. There's something I found out today that you need to hear sitting down."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street, an early example of spatial analysis.
story:
The camping trip was Reilly's idea, which was how Parker ended up sitting on a flattish rock two hours from cell signal with a laptop balanced on his knees. Ms. Ramírez had assigned the GIS project on Thursday and it was due Monday, and Parker had told his mother it was fine, he'd downloaded everything, he'd work offline, he'd still experience nature. Nature, so far, was mostly mosquitoes.

"What are you even doing," Reilly said, dropping a bundle of firewood next to the rock with theatrical exhaustion.

"Flood risk." Parker angled the screen away from the sun. "Ms. Ramírez wants us to overlay two layers for the city and write about what the overlap means. I've got the floodplain map and the housing data."

"That's not camping."

"I'm outside. That's the whole requirement."

Molly came back from the creek with wet sneakers and sat down on his other side, which Parker had mixed feelings about, since she was the one person here who would actually look at the screen. Her aunt lived on Delmar, and every spring the aunt's basement took on water, and every spring the same aunt said the city had promised the drainage would be fixed by the next spring. Molly had opinions.

He layered the maps. The floodplain showed up in blue, the housing layer in a heat gradient, older and cheaper housing darker. Where they stacked, the screen went a color he didn't have a name for, a bruised purple. He zoomed in. Delmar was in the middle of it, along with four other streets Molly could name from memory.

"That's an introduction paragraph right there," Molly said. "Look at that. All the dark stuff is in the blue stuff."

"All the dark stuff is in the blue stuff is not a paragraph," Parker said, but he was thinking about it. Ms. Ramírez had said the hard part wasn't the overlay, it was proving the overlay meant anything. Correlation, she'd called it, and then she'd made them repeat the word like it was a warning label.

Reilly built the fire with the competence of someone who had watched a video about it. "You know what you need," he said, poking the kindling. "One of those things where you say people have been doing maps forever. My brother did that in every essay. Historical hook, guaranteed B."

Parker was already scrolling through his cached browser folder, which was mostly dead links and one PDF he'd saved in a panic Thursday night. It opened. There was a doctor, an old one, and a map of London with little marks on it, and Parker read the first two paragraphs twice because the fire was flickering across the screen and Molly kept leaning on his arm.

"Okay, listen," he said. "In 1854, this physician, John Snow, mapped cholera deaths in London."

"Cholera," Reilly said. "Great start."

"Shut up. He showed the deaths clustered around one water pump. On Broad Street." Parker looked up. "That's it. He just put the deaths on a map and the map did the arguing for him. It's like the first version of what we're doing."

Molly frowned at the screen. "But he knew the pump was the problem. He put the dots where he already guessed they'd be."

"Maybe. Or maybe the dots are what convinced everybody else." Parker turned the laptop so the firelight caught the purple sprawl. "Snow was kind of a polymath, it says here. Did anesthesia too. But the map is what people remember, because the map was the thing a councilman could look at in ten seconds and understand."

They ate freeze-dried pasta and argued about it while the light went down. Reilly's position was that a map was a picture and pictures could lie, and Parker's position was that a picture could lie and still be more honest than a paragraph, and Molly's position was that both of them were ignoring the part where her aunt's basement flooded every year and nobody at the city needed a purple map to know that. "They're not desensitized to it," she said. "They know. Knowing isn't the problem."

Parker kept working after they went to their tents, partly because the deadline was real and partly because Molly's point had opened a hole in his draft. He found a soil layer he hadn't noticed, coverage of ground permeability, and added it. Most of the purple streets sat on ground rated impermeable, which meant the water had nowhere to go and had nowhere to go on the same blocks every single year. That wasn't correlation, exactly. That was mechanism. Or it was the beginning of one. He wrote a sentence and deleted it and wrote it again.

The laptop gave him the low battery warning at eleven. He saved everything, twice, and sat looking at the map while he still could. He had a purple blob, a dead doctor, and an aunt's basement, and he could not yet say in one honest sentence which of those proved anything. But the assignment asked what the overlap meant, not what it proved, and Ms. Ramírez would read either answer, and the grade would be the same either way, and only one of them would be true.

In the morning Molly came out of her tent with her sneakers still damp and stood behind him while he packed the laptop away.

"So did you figure out what you're going to say?"

"I'm going to say the map shows it and I can't prove why."

"That's a terrible intro."

"It's the intro," Parker said, and buckled the last strap.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
Sarah pushed her peas to the rim of her plate and said, "I need to say something to Miya tomorrow and I don't know how to start it."

Her father lowered his fork. Across the table her mother was already tilting her head into that listening posture that made Sarah feel five years old, so she aimed her words at the salt shaker instead. The presentation had gone badly on Tuesday. Miya had promised the slides by Sunday night, and they had arrived at eleven on Monday, half-finished, with two of Sarah's sections missing entirely, so Sarah had rebuilt them at two in the morning and then delivered them stiffly in front of Ms. Dhillon and the whole seminar while Miya sat beside her scrolling her phone. Since then they had exchanged eleven texts, none of them about the presentation, all of them about the weekend.

"I keep drafting it and deleting it," Sarah said. "Every version either sounds like an apology or a lawsuit."

Her father, a raconteur who could stretch a story about a parking ticket into ten minutes, set down his knife in a way that meant he was about to be wise at her. Sarah held up a hand. "I don't want the speech about honesty. I want something that actually works."

"Then eat something and tell us what you've tried," her mother said.

Sarah took a bite to buy time. She had tried writing "you ruined it" in her notes app and then staring at it, because her first instinct was exactly that sentence, blunt and hot. But she'd also watched Zacharie tear into a lab partner last term, precise and cruel, and the partner had simply stopped showing up. Both roads ended somewhere she didn't want to be. She reached into her bag, found her history folder, and pulled out a photocopy she'd made in the library that afternoon, half because she'd needed a citation and half because something in the paragraph had snagged her attention and she couldn't say yet what.

"I found this," she said, flattening the page beside her glass. "There was a psychologist, Thomas Gordon, and in the 1960s he promoted these things called I-messages." Her father opened his mouth and she talked faster. "The idea is you say something like 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late' instead of saying what the other person did to you. Same problem, but it doesn't come out sounding like blame." She looked up. Both her parents had gone quiet in a way that felt less like disapproval and more like curiosity, which was rare enough that she noticed it.

"So you'd say 'I felt stuck' to Miya," her mother said slowly, trying the words out. "Not 'you were late.'"

"It sounds so weak," Sarah said. "That's my problem with it. 'I felt stuck.' It's like handing her a greeting card." She read the photocopy again, hunting for what had snagged her. There it was: the example assumed the listener would ask what happened next. The I-message wasn't the whole conversation, she realized; it was just the door. You opened with the smallest true thing about yourself, and then the other person either walked through it or didn't. That was the part she hadn't understood at the library. She'd been trying to script the entire exchange in advance, to control where it ended, when the whole design of the thing depended on leaving the ending to Miya.

"Say it to us," her father said. "We'll be Miya."

"Dad."

"I'm a very convincing teenage girl." He pulled his water glass toward himself and mimed scrolling a phone, and despite herself Sarah laughed, and her mother laughed, and something in her shoulders came down an inch.

Sarah put her hands flat on the table, the way she did before a pitch in softball. "Miya. Tuesday, when the slides came in late, I felt stuck, because I couldn't practice what I was going to say. And then I rebuilt the two missing sections myself, and I didn't tell you, and that wasn't fair either." She stopped. She hadn't planned the second half of that. It had arrived on its own, and it was true, and it was hers rather than an accusation, and it was pithy in a way none of her drafts had been. Her father lowered the water glass.

"That last part," her mother said. "The part about yourself. That's the part I'd believe if I were Miya."

They made her do it twice more, and the second time her father interrupted mid-sentence to demand whether the slides were going to be late again, which Miya might well do, and Sarah fumbled it, said "you always do this," caught herself, started over with "I get anxious when I don't know the schedule, so could we set a drop-dead time." Afterwards her mother made her collate the versions into a single note on her phone while the details were still fresh, the good lines and the bad ones, so she could read it on the bus in the morning. Sarah did it at the cleared table while the dishwasher hummed. She still didn't know whether Miya would walk through the door or shut it, and she noticed that, for the first time all week, the not-knowing felt less like dread and more like a question she genuinely wanted answered. She typed one last line at the bottom of the note: remember, the small true thing first. Then she carried her plate to the sink and left her phone face-up on the counter, where she'd see the note first thing.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
Maya had the schedule memorized before Ms. Lee finished saying it: Tuesdays and Thursdays, four to eight, Saturdays open to close, seven dollars an hour plus whatever the tip jar surrendered. She signed her name twice on the form, the second signature sloppier, and Ms. Lee slid a green apron across the counter with the ceremony of someone handing over keys to a city.

"Start Saturday," Ms. Lee said. "Fernando will train you on the machine."

Two weeks later, Maya sat at the corner table with her first paycheck and a pencil, because the number on the check was wrong, or the number in her head was, and she intended to find out which. She had worked eleven hours. Eleven times seven was seventy-seven. The check said sixty-nine and some cents, and the pennies mattered less than the principle, which was that eight dollars had gone somewhere she had not authorized.

Tom slid into the chair across from her with his hot chocolate, which he ordered every afternoon though it was nearly June. "You look like you're doing math under duress."

"I am." She turned the check toward him. "Eleven hours. You can do eleven times seven."

"Seventy-seven." He studied the stub below the check, where a small grid of deductions sat in print so fine it seemed designed to escape notice. There was a line for federal income tax, a line for the state, and a line labeled FICA. He tapped that one. "That's your culprit. Six dollars and something."

Maya squinted at it. "What's FICA?"

"No idea. Some old tax thing, my mom maligns it every payday, but she maligns the mailman too, so that tells you nothing." He drank his chocolate and watched Fernando wipe down the espresso machine behind the counter, unhurried, half-dancing to whatever was playing through his earbuds.

She took the pencil back and did the arithmetic the only way she could, backwards. Six dollars and some cents out of seventy-seven. She divided, carried the decimal, and arrived at a number that looked suspiciously clean. "It's 6.2 percent," she said. "Exactly, off by a penny. That's not a rounding error, that's a policy."

"A policy of what?"

"Of taking 6.2 percent of my wages." She flipped the stub over, but the back was blank, which felt like a small insult. Somewhere in the fine print of the world, someone had decided that a portion of every hour she steamed milk would belong to something called FICA, and she had agreed to it, presumably, in the signatures she had scrawled without reading.

Fernando came over on his break and dropped into the third chair, still faintly swaying. "First check?" he said. "Everybody does that face. I did that face. I did that face and then a speech about it, which Ms. Lee let me finish, and then she said the payroll lady handles it and I should get back to the dishes."

"Six dollars," Maya said. "Out of seventy-seven."

"Social Security," Fernando said. "That's what it's for."

"It says FICA."

"Same thing." He stole one of Tom's marshmallows. "It's 6.2 percent, every check, on wages up to a limit for the year. After your wages pass the limit it stops. You won't hit the limit steaming milk here, don't worry."

Maya wrote the number on her napkin, 6.2, and beneath it, up to a yearly wage limit, and beneath that a question mark, because she understood the rule now but not the reason a limit existed at all, and she suspected the reason would take more than a napkin. On one hand, the money was hers, or had been, hours of her life converted to dollars and then skimmed before she touched them. On the other hand, the same skimming touched everyone, Fernando and Tom's mother and presumably Ms. Lee, a whole country of people paying a fraction of every check toward something far off, and there was something almost steadying about that, being included in an obligation before anyone had asked whether she wanted to be. She could hold both views at once. She wasn't sure yet which one would win, or whether they had to compete.

"Deleterious to morale," Tom said, reading her napkin upside down. "That's what my dad calls it when they deduct things."

"It's eight dollars," Maya said. "My morale will convalesce."

Fernando laughed so hard he had to set down the marshmallow. "You two are going to be fun on double shifts."

Ms. Lee came out from the back, counted the drawer with a murmuring that Tom said was her version of whistling, and called across the shop, "Maya, your tips are in the jar if you want them, but if you count them in front of customers they tip less. Learned that from a barista in 1994. She also taught me that everyone deserves one free peccadillo, so take yours now and save the rest for the customers."

Maya went and fished the jar's contents into her palm: four dollars and sixty cents, mostly in quarters. She laid the coins out on the counter in two rows, quarters and the rest, and looked at them for a long moment, her whole first fortnight of work laid flat in metal. Then she swept them into her apron pocket, where they settled against the paycheck, the six-two-tenths percent already gone from that, the tips mercifully untouched, as far as the napkin in her pocket recorded.

"Saturday I open?" she called to Ms. Lee.

"Saturday you open," Ms. Lee said, and slid the key across the counter, small and brass and warm from her hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The rink smelled of burnt pretzels and cold rubber, and Brooke had claimed the corner seat where the glass was clearest, so that when the puck came screaming toward the boards she could feel the shudder in her knees. Her father had bought the tickets in October, before anyone knew the season would end like this, with her cousin's team in the semifinal and half the neighborhood crammed into the standing room behind the net. Kieran was there with his homemade sign, and Dorothy had brought a thermos of cocoa she refused to share until the second period.

The disputed play came with four minutes left in the third. The wing tipped the puck past the goal line, or didn't; even now, replaying it in her head, Brooke couldn't decide which version her eyes had actually seen. The whistle blew, the lights stayed off, the referee's arms went up in that ceremonial shrug that meant deliberation. Around her, the crowd began to chant for the replay screen, that great gray rectangle hanging over center ice like a second, colder moon.

"They have to show it again," Dorothy said, gripping the rail. "That's the whole point of having a screen."

"Is it, though?" Brooke said, and then the screen showed it again anyway, in a frame so tight the puck became a rumor, and the whole arena groaned at once, and a man behind them shouted that from his angle it was clearly in. Brooke found herself wondering whether his angle and her angle and the camera's angle were three different events wearing the same jersey.

At the intermission her father drifted off toward the concession stand, and Ms. Sow, who taught chemistry two doors down from the rink and had come with her nephew, leaned over the empty seat. "You looked like you were about to argue a point," she said. "Go on."

Brooke told her: the puck had crossed the line, probably, but probably felt thin for something this large, this final. She wanted the replay to settle it and she distrusted the wanting, because a slow camera could make anything look like anything if you stared long enough.

"Did you know where the first one came from?" Ms. Sow asked. "The first instant replay on television. CBS, the Army-Navy football game, December 7, 1963. A director named Tony Verna devised the system." She said it the way she said most things, lightly, like leaving a stone on a windowsill for whoever wanted it.

Kieran, who had been eavesdropping shamelessly, turned around. "Sixty years ago people saw a play happen twice and thought the television was haunted?"

"They thought it was a mistake, I think," Brooke said slowly, working it out. "Or a miracle. Nobody had agreed yet that the second seeing was the same as the first." She liked that. She liked how recently it had all been invented, how the ground under the ritual was younger than her grandmother. It made the crowd's chant feel less like a demand and more like a habit still cooling, still sedimentary, layers of argument pressed down into certainty over the years.

"The thing is," Dorothy said, stirring her cocoa with a broken stir stick, "the more we watch the replay, the less we trust our own eyes. Like it desensitizes us to just knowing things."

"That's the wrong direction," Kieran said. "It's the opposite. We used to trust our eyes too much."

"Or both," Brooke said. "We get numb to the original and allergic to the copy at the same time." The buzzer sounded and the teams came back out onto the ice, which had been resurfaced into a pale, perfect steppe, blank and glittering, unmarked by anything that had happened there an hour before. That was the part that kept snagging on her: the ice forgot everything, and the cameras forgot nothing, and she was somewhere in between, holding a memory of a puck she couldn't honestly swear to.

The referees announced their ruling. The goal counted. Half the arena cheered and half booed and Brooke, watching the screen show the tip one more time, in a loop now, from two angles now, realized she still couldn't tell, and that not telling had stopped feeling like failure. She clapped because her cousin's team was going to the final, and because the moment was worth clapping for whether or not it had happened the way the frame insisted.

"Can we get nachos before the handshake line?" Dorothy asked, already standing.

"Only if we get back before they raise the banner," Brooke said, and she squeezed past Kieran's knees, keeping her eyes on the screen as long as she could, where the puck was still hovering there, crossing and not crossing, over and over.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a).
story:
The community centre rented its back room on Tuesdays to anyone with a purpose, and on this particular Tuesday the purpose belonged to six students, a folding table, and a box of day-old doughnuts that Mr. Weiss had brought in a gesture everyone understood as bribery. Eric sat across from Mercedes, who was highlighting her textbook in four colours, and next to Maximus, who had brought a laptop and opened it only to play a recording of rain. The exam was in nine days. Eric had failed the first one, and his father had said nothing about it, which was worse than anything he could have said.

"I still don't get why we're doing this," Maximus said, rotating a pencil between his fingers. "Area under a curve. Who needs the area under a curve."

"Farmers," Mercedes said. "Pilots. People who overdose on purpose."

"That's dark."

"That's physics."

Eric had his notebook open to a page divided down the middle. On the left he'd written rectangles: width 0.1, then 0.05, then 0.01, a marching column of estimates that crept toward some number he couldn't name. On the right, nothing yet. At home the night before, he'd started adding up two hundred rectangles by hand, got lost at the fourth row, and thrown the pencil across the room, where it had lodged behind the radiator, a small casualty he hadn't retrieved.

Mr. Weiss wandered past with his coffee. He was a retired engineer who tutored for free and had a sardonic way of praising people that somehow made them work harder. He looked at Eric's left-hand column, tapped it once, and said, "That's one way to think about it," and moved on. Eric stared at the empty right side and felt the familiar suspicion that there was a door somewhere in the room and that everyone else had walked through it years ago.

"Okay, watch," Mercedes said, turning her book around. She wrote the integral of x squared from 0 to 3, then, beside it, x cubed over 3, and evaluated: 27 over 3, minus 0. Nine. "Two steps. Done."

"That's it?" Eric said. "Where did the x cubed over 3 come from? You just summoned it."

"It's the antiderivative. If F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a." She said it the way she recited her part in the school play, flat and certain, and then she caught herself and laughed. "Sorry. I've been saying that in the shower."

Eric copied the line into his notebook and looked at it. On the left, his rectangles: at width 0.01 the sum had been 8.977 something, straining toward nine but never promising to arrive. On the right, Mercedes's two steps: nine, exactly, the number the rectangles had been circling all along like slow dogs. He checked her antiderivative against his own memory of the derivative rules, x cubed over 3 becoming x squared, and it held. His two columns, which he'd been keeping as rivals, the honest labour of arithmetic versus whatever trickery lived on the right, turned out to be two descriptions of the same territory.

"The rectangles weren't wrong," he said slowly. "They were just doing it the hard way."

"Very hard way," Maximus said. "Tragically hard way. I watched you do that at home over video call, remember. You looked like a man plotting a machination against the rectangle."

"It felt like one."

"So which one do you trust?" Mercedes asked. She wasn't being unkind; her pen was poised, and she genuinely wanted to know. "The two-step thing, or the adding."

Eric thought about his father, who built cabinets and checked every cut twice, and about the exam, which would not wait for two hundred rectangles. He could hold both, he decided: the rectangles to contextualize what the shortcut was actually claiming, so that nine wasn't a magic number but a limit the ugly sums had been crawling toward, and the antiderivative to get him through the exam with time left to check his work. What he couldn't yet explain, even to himself, was why the two methods agreed so neatly, why finding an antiderivative should have anything to do with area at all. Mercedes recited it; Mr. Weiss assumed it; the book asserted it in bold. Eric had verified it once, on one function, and one function was not a proof. He wrote a small question mark at the bottom of the right column and decided he was allowed to keep it there.

Mr. Weiss drifted by again and saw the question mark. He raised an eyebrow but said nothing, which Eric took as a kind of licence.

"Fine," Maximus said, closing the rain sounds and pulling the textbook toward himself. "Teach me the two-step thing. But if you start talking about farmers I'm leaving."

Eric uncapped his pen. "Okay. Same function. You do the rectangles, I'll do the shortcut, and we'll see who finishes first."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
story:
Eva set the pharmacy receipt on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and her chemistry homework, smoothing it flat the way her mother had not bothered to do at the store. 125 over 78, the printout said, in small gray numbers under the time and the store logo. Her mother had waved it off in the parking lot, saying the machines in those places squeezed your arm like an irascible handshake and meant nothing, and then had gone quiet on the drive home in a way that meant it might mean something after all.

Eva had a presentation due Thursday for health class, on interpreting blood pressure readings, and until tonight she had treated it as an assignment she could parametrize into sections: what the two numbers were, what the categories were, what diet and exercise had to do with it. Fill in the boxes, get the grade. Now the boxes had a number in them that belonged to someone she loved, and the assignment had stopped being abstract.

She called Mackenna, who arrived in twenty minutes with her laptop bag and half a bag of pretzels she kept forgetting she owned. They took over the kitchen table, moving the fruit bowl to the counter, and Eva read the printout aloud while Mackenna pulled up the guidelines.

"Okay, so," Mackenna said, scrolling. "There's normal, and then there's elevated, and then stage one, stage two."

"Elevated," Eva repeated, because the word was new in her mouth and she wanted to get it right. Her mother's reading sat there between them on the table, 125 over 78, patient as a held breath.

Mackenna turned the laptop so Eva could see. "Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated means the systolic reading is 120 to 129 with the diastolic below 80." She tapped the screen. "Your mom's systolic is 125. Her diastolic is 78."

"So that's elevated," Eva said slowly, doing the arithmetic of categories in her head. Not normal, and not stage one, but the thing in between, the thing with the mild-sounding name that her mother would hear as a verdict or as nothing at all, depending on how Eva said it.

"It's not a diagnosis," Mackenna said, reading ahead. "It says one reading at a pharmacy doesn't diagnose anything. You'd want it confirmed."

"That's the part I don't know how to say to her." Eva got up and put the kettle on, because her hands wanted something to do, and because her mother would want tea if she came downstairs and found them conspiring over her cardiovascular system. The kitchen window had gone dark, and their reflections sat ghostlike at the table, two girls and a glowing screen.

Tyrone texted around then, because the three of them had split the presentation topics, and his half was the diet and exercise part. He sent a voice memo from his part-time job, the clatter of a dish pit behind him. "So the way I'm framing it, the reading is like a snapshot, right, one frame. Diet and exercise are the movie. You can't tell what the movie's about from one frame, but the frames change if the movie changes." He paused, dishes crashing. "That's as far as I got. Is that even accurate?"

Eva played it twice. It was mostly accurate, she thought, in the way that mattered, though she could hear Ms. Yip, their teacher, asking the question Ms. Yip always asked: what are you certain of, and what are you not? The honest answer was that she was certain of the categories, the thresholds, the way a number slotted into a row. She was not certain what a single machine in a pharmacy could be trusted to say about her mother on a Tuesday evening, and she was not certain how much of what Tyrone called the movie could be rewritten, or how fast.

Her mother came down at nine in her reading glasses, drawn by the kettle, and stood in the doorway with her arms crossed in the gesture she used when she suspected she was being managed. Eva slid the printout across the table before she could decide against it.

"It came back elevated," Eva said, keeping her voice even, unadorned. "That's the actual name for it. Systolic 120 to 129, diastolic below 80, and yours is 125 over 78. One reading, from a machine at a pharmacy." She heard herself laying out the whole fact, the numbers in order, the way you'd hand someone a sealed envelope rather than a rumor. "It's not nothing. It's also not a diagnosis. I think you should get it checked for real."

Her mother sat down and looked at the number for a long moment, glasses low on her nose. Mackenna quietly closed the laptop, an act of tact that Eva noted and would remember. The kettle began to hiss behind them.

"You made tea," her mother said finally. "For a conspiracy."

"For a Thursday presentation," Eva said, getting up to pour. "You're the case study. Unpaid, uncredited, but I promise probity. Full disclosure of methods." Her mother laughed then, short and surprised, and Eva carried the two cups to the table, setting one down in front of the printout so the steam rose over the numbers like weather.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
The tents went up in the last of the light, and Brody discovered that his had a tear along one seam, which was how he ended up sharing with Mathieu, who read climate reports for fun the way other people read box scores. The trip was supposed to be a reward for the debate team, three days by a lake nobody had named on the map, but Ms. Demetriou had brought a folder of graphs anyway, and after dinner she pinned one to a corkboard she'd carried in her pack like a woman who did not trust nature to stay interesting.

The graph showed carbon dioxide across the last century, a line that wandered and then climbed, and Ms. Demetriou said only that they would debate it tomorrow, assigned sides by lottery, and went to wash the pans. Brody got the side defending carbon dioxide as the driver of warming. Mathieu got the side attacking it. "Lucky you," Mathieu said, unrolling his sleeping bag. "I get the fun argument." Brody asked what he meant. "You'll see," Mathieu said, which Brody recognized as the kind of thing a person says when they want to be asked again, so he didn't ask again.

Victoria came over with her flashlight and her notebook, because Victoria prepared for everything, including conversations. She sat cross-legged at the tent flap and asked Brody what he actually knew about the greenhouse effect. He gave her what he had: sunlight comes through, the surface warms, gases slow the escape of heat back out. She nodded slowly, the way she did when she was deciding whether you'd passed. "And which gas matters most?" Brody said carbon dioxide, because that was the one in the news. Victoria smiled and closed her notebook. "Mathieu's going to eat you alive."

He lay awake for a while after she left, listening to the lake make its small sounds against the stones. Mathieu was already asleep, or pretending. Brody thought about the question the way he thought about a chess position, turning it over to see where the trap was. Victoria wouldn't have said that for nothing. He got out his phone, which had one bar of signal near the fire pit, and stood there in the cold reading until the bar disappeared.

The next part he would remember differently, because it was Victoria who told it afterward, standing by the water while the boys set up the debate circle on the flat rock. She had watched Brody at the fire pit past midnight, hunched over his phone, and she thought, not without affection, that this was the trouble with him: he would rather be right than be liked, and he hadn't yet learned that those cost different amounts. She had also seen Ms. Demetriou watching him from her tent, saying nothing, and Victoria wondered what a teacher predicates a decision like that on, whether she was grading preparation or something harder to name, some genus of stubbornness that did well in college and badly everywhere else. Ms. Demetriou had a reputation for being sagacious in a way that showed up only later, when you understood why she'd stayed quiet.

The debate began after lunch. Mathieu stood on the flat rock with the graph behind him and made his move, which was the one Victoria had warned about. "Carbon dioxide isn't even the biggest greenhouse gas," he said. "Water vapor is. It's the most abundant one. So the whole case you're supposed to make is a case about the wrong suspect." He said it lightly, enjoying himself, and a couple of the others nodded, because it sounded like arithmetic and arithmetic sounds like truth.

Brody stood up slowly. His notes were in his pocket and he did not take them out. "Water vapor is a feedback," he said. "That's the word. Warmer air holds more water vapor, so it amplifies warming, but it doesn't start it. The warming gets started by other gases, like carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is the cause; water vapor is what multiplies it." He looked at the graph, at the line going up. "That's why this line matters and the water vapor doesn't have its own line. It's not a driver, it's an echo." The circle was quiet. Mathieu tilted his head, and Brody could see him checking it, the way you check a door to see if it's locked.

"That's actually good," Mathieu admitted. "I don't have an answer to that." Then, because he was Mathieu, he tried a different door. "But how do you know the warming didn't start some other way, and carbon dioxide is just riding along with it?" And there Brody had to stop, because he had read far enough to know the answer existed and not far enough to hold it. "I don't know," he said. "Not from tonight. I know what the graph shows and I know what water vapor does, and past that I'm guessing."

Ms. Demetriou, who had been slicing an apple at the edge of the circle, said nothing about who had won. She asked whether the others thought admitting uncertainty strengthened an argument or weakened it, and let them fight about that for ten minutes while she ate. Later, when the afternoon had gone gold and most of them were swimming, Brody stayed on the flat rock with the graph, tracing the early, wandering part of the line with one finger, the part before the climb, wondering what the air had been doing back then and who had thought to measure it. Victoria came up beside him, dripping, and looked at the same line. "So what's your honest guess," she said. "Riding along, or driving?" Brody kept his finger where it was. "Ask me in ten years," he said. "I'll be the one still standing here."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, the first movement's recapitulation begins unusually in F major, the subdominant, instead of the home key of C major.
story:
Henry spread the photocopied score across the kitchen table, one corner weighted down with a mug that had gone cold an hour ago. The assignment from Ms. Rossi was due Monday: mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation of the first movement of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, and write a paragraph defending each marking. The piece was supposed to be easy. Everyone in class called it the easy sonata, the one beginners learned, and Henry had privately begun to suspect that easy was a dysphemism for something else, though he couldn't yet say what.

He had already bracketed the exposition without trouble. The first theme sat politely in C major, the second theme arrived in G, and the repeat sign closed the section like a gate. The development was harder; Mozart wandered through minor keys so briefly it felt almost gratuitous, like he was only pretending to get lost. Henry pencilled a tentative line where the wandering stopped and the music seemed to settle, then played the recording again on his phone, propped against the sugar bowl.

The doorbell rang at four. Blanche came in shaking rain off her jacket, dropped her bag on a chair, and leaned over the table without asking. "You've marked the recapitulation there," she said, tapping his pencil line. "That's what I got too. Anton says we're both wrong, but Anton also says Ms. Rossi grades on formatting, so."

"Anton wouldn't know a recapitulation if it bit him." But Henry looked at his own line and felt the specific vertigo of a person no longer trusting his own work. He pressed play.

The moment arrived, the one he'd marked: the first theme returning, unmistakable, the same bright little melody. And underneath it, something was off. The accompaniment sat wrong against his ear, like a photograph cropped a hair too closely. He stopped the recording, played the passage again, then again, and finally fetched his mother's old electronic keyboard from the hall closet and set it on the table beside the score.

Blanche watched him hunt for the pitch. "What are you doing?"

"Finding the key." He picked out the melody's first notes with one finger, then held the chord underneath it, and his stomach dropped. It wasn't C. He checked twice, then played the chord for Blanche, then the C major chord above it, back and forth. "The theme comes back in F."

"That's the recapitulation, though. The theme coming back. It has to be the recapitulation."

Henry sat back. "The theme comes back and it's in the wrong key. So either the theme can come back before the recapitulation, or the recapitulation doesn't start where the theme does." He pulled the keyboard closer and played the passage that followed, eight bars, sixteen, listening for the moment F slid back into C like a picture resolving into focus. When it came, it came quietly, without ceremony, and he marked it in the score with a heavier line than he'd used for anything else.

"So Ms. Rossi's paragraph," Blanche said slowly. "You're going to write that everyone in the class would put the line in the wrong place because Mozart does this?"

"I'm going to write that the recapitulation begins in F major. The subdominant." He said the word carefully, the way you handle something borrowed. "Not in C, the home key. Not where the theme returns. Later, when F moves back to C." He looked at his keyboard, at the two chords he'd left ringing in his memory. "I don't actually know why he does it. The paragraph's supposed to defend the marking, not explain Mozart."

"That's going to cost you marks. She wants certainty."

"She wants us to hear it, I think. I can hear it. I can't contextualize it yet, why it works, and I'm not going to pretend I can." He erased his old light line, leaving a faint grey ghost of the wrong answer on the page, and decided not to erase it completely. It was, he thought, part of the map.

Blanche pulled her own copy out of her bag and flattened it beside his. Outside, rain ticked against the window, and the mug had gone so cold that the tea film had settled into a dull skin. She pointed at his ghost line and then at her own identical one. "So both of us heard the theme and stopped listening."

"Both of us heard what we expected." Henry set the phone playing again from the top, softly, and put his pencil down to listen without marking anything. Somewhere in the second minute, Blanche said, "There," and he didn't answer, only tapped the table twice, keeping time with the left hand as it walked home.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The permission slip had been sitting in Ashley's backpack for four days, folded twice, and every time she thought about handing it in she imagined her mother reading the line about the clinic tour. Ms. Nolan had asked for volunteers to train as peer health educators, juniors and seniors who would run the informational table during lunch periods, and Ashley had signed her name before she could talk herself out of it. Now the slip was due, and Ethan was watching her not hand it over.

"You're doing the thing," he said. They were in the second-floor hallway before homeroom, and he was peeling the label off a bottle of water in long slow strips. "The thing where you decide something and then unbeknownst decide the opposite."

"I haven't decided anything."

"You signed the sheet in front of me. I was there. I felt like an acolyte witnessing something."

She gave the slip to Ms. Nolan after first period, sliding it across the desk while the teacher was mid-sentence about photocopies, so it barely counted as a decision at all.

The training happened on Tuesdays in the health classroom, which smelled of chlorine wipes and dry-erase markers. There were six of them, including Melissa, who had signed up because she wanted to be a nurse and said so to anyone who asked. Ms. Nolan gave them folders and a rubber-banded stack of pamphlets and told them the table would open in three weeks, and that they needed to be able to answer questions, not just point at laminated charts.

The trouble started, as Ashley would later think of it, with a pamphlet. Melissa was sorting the contraception ones by type and reading the backs aloud, because Melissa read everything aloud, and she stopped at the condom one.

"Okay, this says ninety-eight percent effective. Why does everyone act like they're, what, a coin flip? Nobody uses them if they're that bad."

Ms. Nolan, who had been at the far side of the room wrestling a projector screen, said only, "Read the front, not the back," and left it there, which Ashley found maddening and, eventually, useful.

The front, in small type under a diagram, did not say ninety-eight percent. It said something about typical use, about thirteen in a hundred over a year, and Ashley read the two figures three times and then a fourth, feeling the floor of something shift slightly beneath her.

"That can't be right," Melissa said. "It says ninety-eight right there."

"That's perfect use," Ashley said slowly. "The back is perfect use. The front is typical use. Typical use, thirteen in a hundred people over a year have an unintended pregnancy, relying only on condoms. Mostly because they're not used correctly every time." She had not known this twenty seconds ago. She was aware of saying it like she had.

"So the box is basically lying?"

"The box is basically telling you the best case." Ashley looked at the pamphlet again, the small honest type, the large flattering type, and thought about every conversation she had ever half-heard in locker rooms and back seats, and how much of it had run on the large type.

Ms. Nolan was closer now, pretending to straighten the pamphlet stack, and Ashley understood that the whole exercise had been set up for them to find this themselves. She wasn't sure whether that made her grateful or annoyed. Possibly both. Ms. Nolan had a way of arranging things so that you did the work and she took none of the credit, which was the opposite of every other adult Ashley knew.

The rest of the training was harder than the pamphlets. Consent, Ms. Nolan insisted, was not a checklist they could hand someone; it was a thing they would have to explain, out loud, to people their own age, some of whom would roll their eyes, one of whom last year had been a senior named Tasha who everyone said had been drunk at a party and about whom everyone had then said too much. Ashley had said too much too, a joke she'd made in the fall that she had been trying to expiate ever since without knowing how, and it occurred to her now that this might be part of how: sitting in this room, learning to say the words properly.

At the clinic tour the following week, a nurse named on her badge only as Dee walked them through the waiting room, the forms, the window where you could ask for testing without explaining why. Melissa asked what it cost and Dee said sliding scale, sometimes nothing, and Ashley memorized the address the way she memorized things for tests, by writing it on her hand.

On the first Tuesday of the table, Ethan came by at lunch, ostensibly for the free mints, and stood reading the condom pamphlet with his eyebrows doing something complicated.

"Thirteen in a hundred," he said. "Huh."

"Typical use," Ashley said. "Only condoms, over a year. Mostly because they're not used correctly every time."

"You have this whole speech now."

"It's not a speech. It's information." She straightened the stack of pamphlets even though it was already straight, and realized she was nervous, and that the nervousness was not about the numbers. A freshman girl had been hovering ten feet away for two minutes, holding her phone, not quite approaching, and Ashley knew with sudden affective certainty that the girl was not there for the mints.

"Go on," Ethan said, and took one for the road.

Ashley pushed the extra chair out from the table with her foot, angling it open, and said, "Hey, do you have a question? You can just sit down, it's totally anonymous, I'm Ashley," and the girl came over slowly, phone still in her hand, and sat, and did not yet say anything at all.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
story:
Samuel had volunteered at the dental office on Marrow Street because Ms. Weber, his neighbor across the fence, had mentioned that her practice needed a front-desk hand on Saturdays, and because his mother thought a college application should subsume some evidence of service, not just grades. He filed insurance forms, learned the word indemnity from a clause in the clinic's liability policy that he read out of boredom on his second Saturday, and made coffee for the garrulous old men who arrived early and narrated their whole lives to anyone in a chair. Then, one October morning, the hygienist asked if he wanted to learn the blood pressure cuff.

"The dentist takes a reading on every new patient," she said, handing him the machine as though it were nothing. "You do it today. Two numbers, top and bottom. Top is when the heart pushes, bottom is when it rests." Trinity and Kaylie had come in for their own cleanings that same morning, booked back to back the way they did everything, and Trinity volunteered her arm first, holding it out across the armrest of the waiting-room chair like an offering.

The cuff hissed and tightened. Samuel watched the display climb and settle: 112 over 74. "That's good," he said, and the hygienist nodded without telling him why it was good, which meant he had to look it up later on his phone in the supply closet, squinting at a chart that put 112 in the normal band. Kaylie's was 118 over 76, and she said, "See, all those walks to the coffee shop are paying off," and Trinity said the walking wasn't the exercise part, the carrying was. He laughed, and then wrote both numbers in the log the hygienist kept, and noticed that he had started to care about numbers he couldn't see or feel.

At noon his grandfather texted him a photo of a fully assembled lawnmower engine, parts he had cleaned and laid out on newspaper like an exhibit. Samuel texted back, and the exchange became the scene he replayed for weeks afterward. His grandfather typed slowly, in complete sentences, a habit from a life of letters. "Doctor's office called about my appointment. They want to check my pressure again. I told them I feel fine, so it must be fine. A man knows his own body."

Samuel stood in the supply closet with the phone in his hand. He had spent the morning learning that a reading of 112 over 74 was a fact about Trinity whether she felt anything or not, that the machine asked the body a question the body never volunteered. He typed, deleted, typed again. "Grandpa, high blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all," he wrote. "It's called a silent killer. They mostly find it by measuring it. Feeling fine doesn't tell you anything." He read it over. It sounded like a pamphlet, but he sent it anyway, then added, "Let them measure it. Then argue with the machine, not me."

The reply came while he was restocking the waiting-room pamphlets. "Silent killer," his grandfather had written. "Dramatic. Your grandmother would have liked that phrase, God rest her dramatic soul." Then, a full minute later: "I will go. And I will take you to that barbecue place after, so you can watch me order the unsalted ribs like an invalid." Samuel grinned at the rack of pamphlets, at the one about sodium and diet, at the one about walking thirty minutes a day, and took two of each for the ride home.

He tried the explaining part on Ms. Weber that afternoon, since she had set the whole thing in motion. She sat behind the front desk with her tea while he told her about Trinity's 112 and his grandfather's texted certainty. "So diet and exercise move the numbers," he said, working it out with his hands, "salt up, walking down, over months, and the numbers move whether the person notices anything or not. Which means you can't trust noticing. You have to measure." She sipped her tea and said only, "You sound like someone who reads pamphlets now," and he said, "I read pamphlets now," and she laughed into her cup.

What stayed uncertain, he admitted to Trinity at school on Monday, was everything else. He didn't know yet whether his grandfather's numbers would come back high, or whether the unsalted ribs were a joke or a surrender, or whether a person could really change a number that had been climbing quietly for years. "Maybe he goes and it's fine," Trinity said, leaning against the row of lockers. "Then he gets to be right for the wrong reason." "That's the worst way to be right," Samuel said, and Kaylie, passing by with her backpack over one shoulder, said, "No, the worst way to be right is alone in your garage feeling fine," and kept walking.

Three Saturdays later his grandfather came in person, unannounced, in his good jacket. He sat in the waiting room with his sleeve already rolled up and told the coffee-drinkers by the window that his grandson worked here, that the boy was going to be a doctor or a lawyer or something with a clipboard. Samuel set up the cuff, and his grandfather held out his arm without being asked, the way Trinity had, and watched the display with an expression Samuel couldn't read, almost like respect. The numbers came up on the screen, and Samuel leaned in close to see them.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: An authentic cadence, a V chord moving to the I chord, sounds final, which is why melodies usually end their last phrase with it.
story:
The music room was spartan by four o'clock: two chairs pushed against the wall, the piano lid open, and a strip of January light crossing the staff paper where William had written eleven bars. He needed sixteen by Friday, when Mr. Adeyemi would collect the assignments for the winter showcase, and the melody kept undulating past the bar lines like it had somewhere better to be. I had it finished two days ago, he told himself, which was not quite true; what he had was a first phrase he liked and a lie of convenience about the rest.

Emmanuelle came in with her violin under her arm and a paper bag of clementines, because she believed the room was hers on Thursdays, and because she was often right. "Play it," she said, before he could cover the page. She had a way of asking that wasn't asking.

He played the eleven bars. They sounded smaller than they had in his head, which was usual, but they were not bad; the chords moved the way Mr. Adeyemi had sketched on the board, from the one chord to the four and back, and the tune rose over the four like a question. He ended where the ink ended, on the five chord, mid-air.

"It doesn't sound finished," Emmanuelle said. She took a clementine and began peeling it with her thumbnail. "It sounds like you stopped, not like it ended."

"It ends Friday whether it sounds finished or not."

"That's a deadline, not an ending." She set the peel in a coil on the piano. "Mr. Adeyemi did a whole thing on this. An authentic cadence, the five chord moving to the one chord, sounds final. That's why melodies usually end their last phrase with it." She said it the way she said most things, as though handing him something she'd already gotten tired of carrying.

William looked at his bar eleven, the five chord sitting there already, and felt the strange pleasure of a problem that had been solved before he'd understood it existed. All he had to do was resolve it, land the tune on the root, and the melody would close itself like a door. He wrote bar twelve: the one chord, the tonic, the note the whole piece had been leaning toward.

It sounded terrible.

He played it again to be sure. The finality was there, undeniably, but it arrived four bars early and flattened everything before it, the way a word repeated too soon loses its meaning. He erased bar twelve, and the eraser smeared the ledger lines, and he sat looking at the smear while Emmanuelle practiced her shifts in the corner, her violin line moving up and up and settling.

Here is where I should admit something. I had told Lorelai at lunch that composing came easily to me, that the assignment was basically done, and I had almost believed it. What actually came easily was the first phrase, the part that needed no ending because it was all beginning. The hard part was not writing sixteen bars; the hard part was making the last four earn the five chord I'd already placed, so that the resolution would feel like arrival instead of triage. Lorelai had asked what a cadence even was and I'd said, too smoothly, oh, it's obvious. It was not obvious. It was a fact you had to grow into, like a proof in geometry where the lemma looks trivial until you try to build anything on it.

Emmanuelle stopped playing. "Try delaying it," she said. "Make the last phrase circle first. Then the five, then the one."

So he did. Bars twelve through fourteen wandered back toward the tune's opening, a quiet return, and bar fifteen set the five chord under the melody's highest note, holding it like a breath, and bar sixteen fell to the tonic on the first beat, simple and square. He played all sixteen for her, his hands cold on the keys, and the ending landed with a click he could feel in his teeth. It sounded finished. Whether it sounded good, he honestly could not tell anymore; his ears had been inside it too long.

"Better?" she asked.

"I don't know yet. Ask me after Friday."

Emmanuelle gathered her clementine peel, folded it into the bag, and slung the violin over her shoulder. At the door she paused. "It sounded finished to me," she said. "That's the part I'd trust." Then she was gone down the hallway, and William copied his rough page onto clean staff paper, writing the last bar slowly, twice, so the ink would be dark enough to see from the back of the room.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and cold radiators, and Isabelle had claimed the folding table nearest the bleachers because it was the only one with a whiteboard she could carry. On it she had drawn six columns, one for each week before the season started, and she was filling them with numbers: 20 miles, 22, 24.2, 26.6. Her pen paused at the fourth week and she recalculated twice, because 26.6 plus ten percent came to 29.26, and she refused to write 29.3.

"You're doing math on a Friday," Omar said, dropping his bag beside the table. He had come in from the track with his hood up and his cheeks still red, and he leaned over the whiteboard without asking, which was his way. "What's the ten percent thing?"

"It's the rule," Isabelle said. "You never raise your weekly running distance more than ten percent from one week to the next. That's how you avoid getting hurt. It's basically science."

"Basically science," Omar repeated, in the tone he used for things he intended to look up. He sat down on the table's edge, which Ms. Tang had told them a hundred times not to do, and picked up her pen to tap it against his knee. "Where'd you find it?"

"Everywhere. It's a popular guideline. Every running site has it." She took the pen back. She had spent three evenings on it, building the season out like a staircase, each step exactly one tenth higher than the last. The neatness of it had felt like proof. Her shin had ached all last season, a congenital-seeming complaint she'd blamed on her flat feet, and she had promised herself this year would be structured, graduated, safe. The plan was almost finished. Only the taper week was blank.

Omar pulled out his phone anyway, thumbs moving, and she watched him do it and hated that she watched him do it, because if the rule were as solid as she believed, the search would only confirm it, and she wanted the confirmation more than she wanted to be right. "Huh," he said.

"Huh what?"

"So there's this study. Studies, plural." He turned the screen toward her, and she took it, and the bleachers behind her creaked as Trace came down them two steps at a time with a water bottle she'd already half finished. "They looked at whether the ten percent rule actually prevents injuries," Omar said. "It doesn't beat other gradual plans. Like, people who increased by ten percent max got hurt about the same as people who followed different, also gradual, schedules."

Isabelle read the summary twice. The words did not rearrange themselves into something kinder. "That can't be right."

"That's what it says."

She looked at her whiteboard, at the six obedient columns with their decimal-pointed ascents, and felt the peculiar vertigo of discovering that a law she had been obeying was only a habit many people shared. Trace leaned in over her shoulder, reading the numbers upside down with the ease of someone who did crosswords in her head.

"So don't spike it and you're fine," Trace said. "Gradual is gradual."

"It's not that simple," Isabelle said, and then stopped, because it might be that simple, and the not-knowing was the actual problem. She was not used to planning inside uncertainty. In chemistry the rules either held or you'd made an arithmetic error. Here the rule held and also didn't, the way a handrail could be solid and still not prevent every fall.

From where Omar sat, the whole thing looked smaller than Isabelle's face was making it.
