He watched her stare at the numbers, and he thought about his own seasons, the autumns when he had done nothing all summer and then let the coach's first two weeks acclimate his legs through pure soreness, the year he'd strained his hamstring and the year he hadn't, no pattern he could name in either. He had always assumed the people with plans knew something he didn't. Watching Isabelle cross out 29.26 with one firm stroke, he understood that she was further along than him in a direction he'd thought was a wall.

"Not the numbers," she said, mostly to herself, and pulled the marker from the tray. She wrote rest days into the columns first, actual full days, then warm-ups before the harder sessions, ten minutes of drills she'd always skipped as a waste. Then she rebuilt the mileage, and it came out crooked: 20, 22, 24, then a down week at 18, then 26, then another dip. It looked like a mistake. She wrote it anyway, because a plan you knew was approximate could bend when your shin spoke up, and a plan you thought was law could only be obeyed or abandoned.

Ms. Tang came through on her rounds with her keys jangling and paused at the board. "Who taught you the down weeks?"

"Nobody," Isabelle said. "I made them up."

"Good," Ms. Tang said, and kept walking, and Trace grinned as if a coin had been dropped in her.

Omar slid off the table, finally legal, and picked up his bag. "So all that math for a plan you invented."

"I didn't invent rest," Isabelle said, capping the marker.

"No," he agreed, heading for the door. "You invented the decimals."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scores 180 countries and counts concentration of media ownership as one pressure on press freedom.
story:
The argument started, as most of them did, with Josiah pasting a link at eleven at night. The story was about the harbor development, the one that would replace the boatyard with a hotel and a parking structure, and the headline called it a "boost for the waterfront." William read it twice, then typed that it read like an advertisement. Josiah replied with a single eye-roll emoji, which William found loquacious in its way, saying more than a paragraph would have.

"It's the Herald," Ephraim chimed in, from wherever Ephraim was at eleven-fifteen on a Tuesday. "The Herald is a real newspaper. My grandpa reads it."

"Everything's a real newspaper if someone prints it," William typed, then deleted it, then typed something worse and deleted that too. What he finally sent was: "who owns it though." Nobody answered for a while. He could picture Josiah leaning back from his phone, insulted, and Ephraim googling "who owns it."

Ephraim, who was nothing if not thorough, came back eight minutes later with a screenshot. The Herald had been bought three years ago by a group that also owned the company building the hotel. Not the same company, exactly, but the same people at the top, the way two shirts from the same closet belong to the same guy. "so it's a coincidence," Josiah wrote, and then, before anyone could respond, "you can't just say everything's biased whenever you lose an argument. That's your whole move. You prognosticate that the news is corrupt and then you're shocked when you're right."

William wanted to point out that being right wasn't the flaw in his reasoning, but Josiah was already gone, posting instead about Friday's game. That was the trouble with Josiah, and also, William had to admit, the reason arguing with him never got boring: he treated a loss in one thread like a defeat in all of them, some private nemesis tally that only he could see.

The next day in Ms. Romano's class, William still had it in his teeth. She had assigned a short paper on "a claim and its sources," due the following week, which everyone had treated as a formality until now. William stayed after the bell and asked, carefully, whether ownership counted as a source question or whether that was cheating, getting at the money instead of the words. Ms. Romano said that sounded like a paper, and that if he wanted a place to start, Reporters Without Borders kept an index. She wrote nothing on the board. She did not elaborate. He appreciated that about her.

He looked it up that night in the group chat, half for the paper and half to finish the fight. The World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scored 180 countries, and it counted concentration of media ownership as one of the pressures on press freedom. It was right there on the page, listed alongside other pressures, as if it were a normal thing to measure. William had assumed bias was something you had to catch red-handed, a slip or a favor. The index treated it more like weather, a condition a country could have more or less of. He screenshotted it and sent it to the chat with no caption, which he felt was the most honest form of gloating.

Josiah's sister, who was doing an exchange year in Finland and lurked in the chat under the name her parents gave her at birth, replied first. She said she'd checked Finland's rank after a teacher mentioned the index, and it was near the top, and that she'd read the ownership part before she understood why it mattered. "I thought it was about how many papers a country has," she wrote. "It's about who has how many."

Ephraim said that was the same thing, and William said it wasn't, and Josiah typed "can we not," and then, a minute later, "fine. so the Herald story. what do we do, not read it?" That was the question William had been circling all night. Not reading it felt like the wrong answer, and reading it uncritically felt worse, and he had a page and a half of paper due on exactly that knot.

He typed that he didn't know yet, that maybe the point was reading it the way you'd listen to a guy reviewing his own hotel. Josiah replied with a thumbs up, then a second one, then the eye-roll emoji again, softened somehow by the thumbs-ups on either side of it. William set his phone face-down on the desk, opened a blank document, and wrote the Herald's headline at the top, followed by a single question mark.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906.
story:
Avery had the database open and her outline printed before the bell for last period had finished ringing, but the outline was a lie. It said, in her own handwriting from Sunday night, that Victorian workhouse children were "completely destitute and abandoned by society," and she had known even then that the sentence was decoration, not argument. The paper was due at eight the next morning. Ms. Wright had said it twice and then a third time in the doorway: an argument, footnotes, a bibliography, a standard citation style, no exceptions.

Jaden dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of books he had clearly not read. "I'm doing mine on whether athletes should be able to monetize their image in college," he said. "My argument is yes. That's an argument, right?"

"It's an opinion."

"Same thing."

"It's not." She turned her laptop so he could see the database. "Watch. Workhouse children were destitute, and I can prove that with a source. But so what? A thousand people have written that. The argument has to be the part where I say something they'd argue with."

He frowned at her screen. "So what's yours?"

"I don't know yet. That's the problem."

Chad arrived ten minutes later, sat down, and immediately began fighting with the citation guide Ms. Wright had handed out. "Why does it have to be footnotes," he said. "Who invented footnotes. Like a actual person sat down and decided we all have to do this."

"Look it up," Avery said, mostly to make him stop talking, and he did, typing with two fingers, narrating his search. It took him under a minute.

"The Chicago Manual of Style," he read. "It's got the whole footnote system. And get this, it says the University of Chicago Press published it first in 1906."

"1906 like a hundred years before my phone," Jaden said.

"Older than your great-grandparents," Chad said, and slid the laptop back toward Avery as if the fact were her fault.

She wrote the sentence down in her notes, for no reason she could have defended. Then she looked at it. A style guide, older than everyone in the building, still telling seventeen-year-olds where to put a period. She opened the notes-and-bibliography section and began formatting her first footnote, and the tedium of it, the indentation, the page number, the exact order of things, was almost comforting. Someone in 1906 had decided that this was how you showed where your evidence came from. That was not decoration. That was the whole point, she realized, pressing the heels of her hands into her eyes. Footnotes were not a hoop. They were the paper saying, out loud, I am not making this up.

The library emptied in waves. At five, Jaden left with his image-rights thesis still shapeless. At five thirty, Chad left, having discovered that his bibliography was alphabetized wrong and blaming the University of Chicago Press personally. Avery stayed.

She had seven sources on the workhouses and a growing pile of arguments she could not make herself believe. The parish officials who ran the system had believed they were reforming pauperism, not inventing cruelty; the reformers who exposed it had sometimes exaggerated, and had still been right about the important things. Her outline wanted her to pick a villain. The sources refused to give her one.

Ms. Wright came through at six to reshelve the atlas and paused at Avery's table. "Finding an argument?"

"I found two," Avery said. "One is that the system failed because the people running it measured poverty as a moral problem. The other is that it failed because it was underfunded and nobody could have made it work. I keep going back and forth."

"That sounds like a paper."

"It sounds like I can't decide."

"Then write the version where you can't decide," Ms. Wright said, "and tell me which one survives. That's different from not having an argument. I'll be in my office until seven."

Avery worked until the windows went dark. She drafted the moral-failure version and it collapsed in the third paragraph; the underfunding version collapsed faster. What survived was smaller and harder to say: that the system's cruelty and its ideology were the same thing, inseparable, and that the evidence for one was evidence for the other, though she could not prove they were the same and would not pretend she could. She footnoted every claim. Page numbers, indentation, exact order. Her sixty-third footnote, when she counted them, was formatted the way a manual first published in 1906 said it should be, and she thought of that fact the way you think of a handshake from someone very old.

She saved the file twice, emailed it to herself, and packed her bag. At the door she stopped, went back, and crossed out the sentence in her own handwriting from Sunday night. Then she pulled the door closed behind her and heard the lock catch.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The screen above the bar filled the whole back wall of Marconi's, and by the second period every booth was full. Megan sat wedged between her mother and Phoenix, wings going cold in the middle of the table, watching her grandfather hold court from the head. He had been coming to Marconi's for thirty years, and he treated the big screen like a guest he personally had invited.

"Nineteen seventeen," he said, tapping the table with two fingers. "That's when the Cup started. I remember my father telling me."

Elliot leaned over his drink. "Weren't you born in nineteen fifty?"

"The Cup's older than grandpa," Megan said, before she could stop herself. "I did a project on it in eighth grade. It was donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston. First awarded in 1893." She hadn't thought about the poster in years, silver foil glued onto bristol board, but the numbers had stayed put. "It's the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America. That's the whole point of it."

Her grandfather's jaw shifted. "Oldest trophy. What about baseball."

"Trophy," Megan said. "For a team. It's not the pennant." She felt her mother's hand press flat against her knee, one of those signals that traveled through the family without anyone admitting it was a language.

Under the table, Phoenix's phone buzzed against Megan's hip. It was Phoenix's phone, actually, handed over at the door because Phoenix could not be trusted to leave it alone during a crisis. The screen said: 2nd intermission. We go NOW or we miss my slot. The open mic across town started at nine, and Phoenix had been rehearsing a set for three weeks, pacing Megan's bedroom with index cards, performing for the mirror and the closet door.

"One more period," Megan whispered.

"You said that at the first intermission."

"It was true then too."

Phoenix's set was scathing, that was the whole design of it, a ten-minute takedown of places like this one, sports bars that commodify belonging and sell it back with a cover charge. Phoenix had made Megan promise to be in the third row. Megan had promised. But the third period was starting, the game was tied, and her grandfather was still holding his jaw at an angle that meant he was deciding whether to be wrong in public.

"Grandpa," she tried, "it's not a fight. Lord Stanley was the Governor General. He bought a bowl for about fifty dollars and donated it." She stopped there. She had almost said he bought it so the best team could have it, and she could hear the essay voice coming on, the one that made Elliot call her Professor Whitlow. She picked up a wing instead.

"Eighteen ninety-two," her grandfather said slowly, like he was testing ice. "So my grandfather could have watched the first one."

"Your grandfather was born in eighteen ninety-eight," Megan's mother said.

"He could have heard about it." He said it with such dignity that Elliot laughed into his napkin, and even the waiter, refilling the basket, smiled at the ceiling.

Phoenix leaned in close to Megan's ear. "This is a dialectic, not a game. Two sides, one truth, somebody wins. You're choosing the side with buffalo sauce on it."

"It's overtime rules," Megan said. "It doesn't work like that." But she was already doing the math in her head: forty minutes to the open mic if they left during intermission, twenty if they left now and ran, zero if the game went to overtime. Grandpa wasn't asking her to stay. He hadn't asked for anything in years, that was the problem, he'd stopped asking and started announcing. And yet he'd said eighteen ninety-two back to her like it was something he was trying on, not something he was surrendering.

"Go," her grandfather said, not looking away from the screen. "Your friend's thing. I watched hockey before you were born and I'll watch it after."

"He's really not that old," Megan said, but she was already sliding out of the booth, Phoenix grabbing the index cards and the phone, Elliot waving them off with a fry held like a tiny baton.

They ran the four blocks and got there at nine sharp, and the room was mostly empty chairs, and the host said the open mic ran long tonight, the featured act was still on. Phoenix went to sign up. Megan sat in the third row and pulled up the game on her phone: overtime, tied, and then a scramble in front of the net, and the lamp lit, and the screen at Marconi's, which she could not see, was surely showing her grandfather on his feet. A text arrived from Elliot: he made the waiter put your name on the check. Says the historian drinks free.

The host tapped the mic. "Next up, doing comedy, Phoenix."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
story:
Maika sat at the kitchen table with a biology worksheet, a highlighted textbook, and her phone face down beside a bowl of cereal she had stopped eating. The worksheet asked her to explain, in her own words, how DNA gets copied and how a gene becomes a protein. She had written two sentences, crossed out one, and then underlined a word in the textbook so hard the pen went through the page.

Her mother passed through the kitchen carrying laundry and paused at the counter long enough to say that the test was Monday, and that Maika's aunt had failed biology twice, so it ran in the family. Maika said that was not how genetics worked. Her mother said whatever it was, it ran in the family, and went upstairs.

The front door opened without a knock, which meant Harley. He had a soda from the corner store and a takeout container of pond water he had collected that morning for a different class, and he set both on the table without asking. He leaned over her worksheet. "You look like the worksheet won," he said.

"It's about copying DNA," Maika said. "There's an enzyme that starts it, and I keep losing track of which one does what." She turned the textbook so he could see the diagram, a ladder twisted into a helix, rungs labeled with letters.

Harley drank his soda and looked at the diagram for a while. Then he reached for the container of pond water, set it on the textbook page, and looked at something moving in it, a water flea or whatever it was, small and busy. Behind it, on the page, the helix waited to be explained. He said, "Okay, so the ladder. Before the ladder can be copied, something has to open it. Like this." He took hold of the zipper on his jacket and pulled it down slowly, tooth by tooth, the halves separating in a widening V.

"That's it," Maika said. She pulled the textbook back and found the paragraph. "The enzyme is helicase. It unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together." She read the line out loud, then once more to herself. "So that's the first step. Everything else, the copying and the reading, happens after that. It has to open before it can be copied." She wrote it on the worksheet in her own words, checking the paragraph to make sure she had the order right: helicase, then the copying.

The apartment door buzzed again and it was Audrina, who had a printout of a quizlet set and a complaint about Ms. Farah-Ali assigning this before teaching it. Audrina sat down, arranged her flashcards, and said the whole thing was memorization, transcription and translation, a parade of vocabulary. Maika said she did not think it was only that. "Transcribe means to copy something across," she said. "Translate means to put it into another language. My dad used to do transcription for court cases. Same word." She had looked up the etymology that morning, half avoiding the worksheet, and it had actually helped: the gene gets copied into a message, and then the message gets read into protein.

Audrina, who was loquacious when she was nervous, talked through three cards in a row without pausing, and Maika let her, because talking it through was how Audrina learned, the way unzipping a jacket was apparently how Harley learned. It occurred to Maika that she did both: she needed the story and the word. Harley's jacket gave her the picture, and the textbook's sentence gave her the exact truth of it, and she had to hold them together, because the picture alone would let her interpolate all kinds of things that were not in the book, like imagining the enzyme chewing through the ladder instead of just opening it.

"Say the whole thing," Audrina said. "Once, out loud. If you can say it, you know it."

Maika put her hand flat on the textbook. "The enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs. Then the DNA gets copied. Then one gene gets transcribed into a message, and the message gets translated into a protein." She heard her own voice slow down on the second sentence. "I still don't fully get the translation part," she said. "The message part. There's something about how it's read in groups of three, and I have that card somewhere."

"That's Monday's problem," Harley said. He held the pond water up to the ceiling light, and the water flea drifted across the diagram, crossing the unzipped helix, then past it, into the margin.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: A 2008 trial in Norway found that young female soccer players aged 13 to 17 who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall.
story:
Hailey printed the training plan at the school library because the printer at home was out of ink, and she folded it into quarters and put it in the pocket of her shorts before riding her bike to the track. It was Sunday evening, which the plan marked as a rest day, and she had chosen Sunday deliberately, reasoning that nobody would be there and she could lay the whole thing out on the bleachers and see if it worked. Fourteen girls on the spring team, six weeks before the regional meet, and until now the warm-up had been whatever anyone felt like doing, usually a lap and some stretching that Gabriela once described as decorative.

The plan had come out of an argument. On Thursday, Gabriela had said that warm-ups were superstition, that you either were the kind of runner who got hurt or you weren't, and Hailey had gone home annoyed enough to look it up. She found a study from 2008 in Norway. Young female soccer players, thirteen to seventeen, who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall. She read it twice, then read the parts around it, and the parts around those, and by eleven she had a notebook with columns for Monday through Sunday.

She was pinning the pages to the chain-link fence with clothespins when Gabriela and Sally came around the corner of the grandstand, both in cleats, both clearly having planned to run.

"It's a rest day," Hailey said.

"It's Sunday," Sally said. "Sunday is when we run."

Hailey held up the first page. On it she had written Monday, tempo work, twenty minutes, followed by the warm-up, and she had written the warm-up out in full, fifteen minutes of it, running drills and single-leg work and nordic curls, because the program she was building from called itself structured and she was not going to pretend otherwise. Tuesday said easy distance. Wednesday said intervals. Thursday said rest. "The body adapts on rest days," she said. "That's not my opinion. That's the whole basis of it."

Gabriela squinted at the fence. "Fifteen minutes of warm-up. Before we've even started." She said it the way people say a price they have no intention of paying.

"About a third fewer injuries," Hailey said. "There was a trial in Norway, 2008. Soccer players, girls, our age, thirteen to seventeen. The ones who did the FIFA 11+ had about a third fewer injuries overall. Total. Not just knee things, everything."

Sally had come closer and was reading over the word nordic, mouthing it. "Our age," she repeated.

"Our age exactly," Hailey said.

Gabriela sat down on the bottom bench and pulled off one cleat and shook a pebble out of it, taking her time. Hailey recognized the maneuver; Gabriela did this whenever she was changing her mind and wanted it to look like something else was happening. Hailey had spent half of Friday night thinking about why the number had captivated her so completely, and she had decided part of it was extrinsic, that she liked having a statistic to swing like a club, and that part of it was simpler, that if Sally pulled her hamstring again in the first week of June, like last year, Hailey would have to watch it happen from the second turn, again. She could not fully separate the two motives and had stopped trying. Her mother had quoted the old adage about leading a horse to water, which Hailey found useless, since nobody was being led anywhere; they were all just standing at a fence looking at paper.

"Who does the nordic things?" Gabriela said, putting the cleat back on.

"Everyone. That's the point. It's a program, not a menu."

"And Thursday we do nothing."

"Thursday we do nothing."

Gabriela stood, walked to the fence, and took down the Wednesday page, the one with the intervals, and studied it with her head tilted. Then she took down Thursday, then Sunday, which said only rest in Hailey's handwriting, nothing else, and laid all three on the bleacher seat side by side. She put her finger on Sunday. "What do people do on a rest day, actually. If they're not running."

"Whatever they want," Hailey said. "That's the whole day."

Sally laughed, and Gabriela didn't, but she got her phone out and photographed the fence, top to bottom, four shots, and Hailey heard the shutter go each time. Then Gabriela put the clothespins back on the pages she'd removed, pressing each one until it held, and said, "Sixty seconds, and if you're lying about Norway we're running Sundays forever." She stepped onto the track and started the first drill, and after a moment Sally followed, and Hailey stood at the fence holding the notebook, watching to see whether they did it right.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Islamic law, ijtihad is the independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts do not directly answer.
story:
The kettle had been on since noon, and by three the tea at the bottom of Alexa's cup had gone turbid, milk skin curling against the ceramic. She sat at her aunt's dining table with the debate prompt in front of her: whether the Quranic prohibition on riba, usury or interest, still applied in a world of mortgages, student loans, and credit cards. The regional final was in nine days. Her aunt's house was the only quiet place she knew on Saturdays, because everyone else was in the kitchen arguing about whose turn it was to host next month.

Rosemary arrived first, shaking rain off her jacket, then Brycen, who lived three streets over and came mostly for the food. They spread out their evidence: photocopied verses, a hadith about the lender and the borrower, two opposing op-eds from the school library database. Brycen had drawn a line down a napkin and written STILL APPLIES on one side and OBSOLETE on the other, as though the question were a matter of arithmetic.

"Here's my problem," Alexa said, tapping the verse about doubling and redoubling debt. "Everyone at school will say, that was then, this is now. And if I just quote the text harder, I sound like I'm hiding from the modern world. If I concede everything, I sound like I don't believe the text matters at all." The problem had begun to metastasize in her mind over the past week, spreading from riba into every rule she'd ever been taught, so that she couldn't look at her mother's bank statement without a small cold doubt.

Rosemary, who was spreading cheese on bread with more attention than it required, said, "My cousin took us to a thing at the community hall last month. Islamic finance talk. This kid stood up, maybe fourteen, and asked how scholars rule on online banking when it didn't exist in the texts."

"What did the speaker say?" Alexa asked.

"That's what ijtihad is for," Rosemary said. "Independent reasoning. A qualified scholar uses it to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts don't directly answer." She said it the way she repeated things her cousin told her, slightly too fast, then went back to the bread.

Alexa wrote the word down. She asked the aunt's permission to use the desktop computer in the hallway, the old one that hummed like a refrigerator, and spent an hour reading. She was no savant; the classical Arabic terms slid off her, and twice she had to retrace her steps through a footnote that pointed to another footnote. But she began to see a shape. The prohibition on riba wasn't being discarded by the people she was reading, nor clung to word for word. It was being reasoned from, stretched over new cases, argued over by people who disagreed with each other in long, courteous, furious letters.

She came back to the table and rearranged the napkin. On Brycen's line she wrote a third column, nothing in it yet, and said, "I think the whole frame is wrong. The question isn't does the rule still apply. The question is how the rule gets applied when the world changes. If I argue that, I'm not running from the text, and I'm not freezing it either."

"Judges want a side," Brycen said. He was probably right. The rubric, printed on the back of the prompt, awarded points for a clear position. Alexa looked at the rubric, then at her third column, and felt the pull of choosing the easy shape for her argument, the shape that would score well and leave her dishonest.

"Then my side is that it applies, but the application is reasoning, not photocopying," she said. "Somebody has to do the work of deciding what interest means in a mortgage. That work has a name and a tradition behind it. That's my case."

"Did you just call my napkin a photocopy?" Brycen said, and Rosemary laughed so hard she had to set down the bread.

The kitchen emptied toward evening as the aunts and uncles dispersed to their own homes, carrying foil containers. Ms. Fortin, the neighbour who had come by for the leftover curry, stood in the doorway with her umbrella and asked what the three of them had been working at all afternoon. Alexa gathered the photocopies, the napkin with its third empty column, the page where she'd written ijtihad and beneath it, in her small handwriting, not sure yet.

"A debate," she said. "I'm still building it."

"Good," Ms. Fortin said. "The unbuilt ones turn out best." She opened the umbrella on the porch and stepped into the rain.

Alexa sat back down and uncapped her pen.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
Camille set the plywood board across two sawhorses in her backyard and began sorting the jar of broken tiles by color. She was making a mosaic for Ms. Janssen, the neighbor whose fence backed onto the yard, because Ms. Janssen had given her the tiles in the first place, along with the grout and the bruised tin of adhesive, and had asked only one thing: that it be a landscape.

Karissa arrived at noon with a paper bag of cherries and opinions. She stood over the board with her shoes in the grass and said the horizon should go a third of the way down.

"Who made that rule?" Camille said.

"It's just the rule," Karissa said. "Ms. Janssen probably knows it. It's called the rule of thirds. Everybody uses it."

Camille had sketched the design that morning in pencil on the board: a field, a line of trees along the back edge, a sky pressed flat and gray. She had drawn the horizon in the middle without thinking, the way a child draws a house with a door in the center. She looked at the sketch now and could not tell whether the middle was wrong or whether it was only unpopular.

"Everybody isn't a reason," she said.

Karissa spat a cherry pit into her hand. "Fine, put it in the middle, and Ms. Janssen will lambaste you in that polite way she has, and you'll regrout the whole thing."

Camille did not put it in the middle. She also did not put it a third of the way down. She left the pencil line where it was and started laying tiles for the field, working from the bottom edge upward, blues and greens she had decided were a river and its bank, though she had not told anyone that. The field could wait. The horizon could wait. It was a line she could draw last, once she knew what the mosaic wanted under it.

On Thursday Emie came over with her laptop to work on a college application essay, and after twenty minutes of the essay she gave up and sat on the grass beside the board. Camille had covered a third of the plywood now, and the empty upper part looked less like sky than like a question.

"Some art guy," Emie said, scrolling. "Hold on. John Thomas Smith. It's in a book. Remarks on Rural Scenery, 1797. He wrote the phrase down first, rule of thirds. Somebody on this forum says so, and there's a scan of the actual page."

Camille leaned over the screen. The scan was faint, the old type crowded, but there were the words. "1797," she said. "That's it? One man, one book?"

"That's what it says. First written down. Which doesn't mean invented, probably, but nobody wrote it earlier, as far as this person can tell."

Camille sat back. She had assumed the rule was like gravity, discovered rather than decided, and now she was holding the possibility that it was more like a property line, an agreement that worked only because people kept honoring it. One man had looked at paintings and ponds and hills and written down a proportion, and two hundred years later Karissa repeated it in a backyard as law.

"So it's a preference that got old," Camille said.

"It's a preference that survived," Emie said. "Those aren't the same thing."

They argued about it mildly while Camille laid tiles for the tree line, small dark rectangles she nudged into rows until they suggested the arboreal edge of a wood without drawing every trunk. Emie held the laptop away from the grout dust. When she left, she left the forum page open on Camille's kitchen table, and Camille read the thread twice, including an argument between two strangers about whether the rule was a tool or a cage, which ended, as those arguments usually did, with no winner and a link to a book on composition.

Saturday, Ms. Janssen leaned on the fence with her tea. She had been watching the mosaic grow all week without comment. Now she asked what the dark band was.

"The trees," Camille said.

"And where's the horizon?"

Camille showed her the pencil line, still in the middle, though she had since measured the board and made two small pencil ticks, one at a third from the top and one at a third from the bottom, so that both options sat on the wood like charges waiting to be chosen. She told Ms. Janssen about John Thomas Smith, the book, the year, the phrase written down first, and how knowing that had not settled anything for her.

"It made it heavier, honestly," Camille said. "If it were true the way math is true, I'd just follow it. But it's a choice somebody made, and it lasted, and I can't tell if that means it's good or just old."

Ms. Janssen drank her tea. "You know what I think indemnity is, in insurance? A payment that makes you whole after a loss. There's no equivalent for mistakes in art. You just get the mistake."

"That's comforting," Camille said, and meant it partly.

"It's not meant to be either."

That evening Karissa came back, and Camille finally drew the horizon. She set it below both pencil ticks, lower than Smith would have wanted, low enough that the sky took almost everything and the field was a strip, the trees a dark interruption. It was not a compromise between the middle and the third. It was a third decision, arrived at by refusing the first two, and when she stepped back onto the patio she could see that the mosaic had stopped looking like a landscape drawn from life and started looking like weather about to happen.

Karissa looked at it a long time. "I hate that I kind of like it," she said.

Camille picked up the grout float. "Hold the board steady."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The three primary chords of a major key are built on its first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major they are C, F and G.
story:
Quintin arrived at four with his guitar and a bag of chips he didn't offer to share, and he set both down in Grayson's bedroom like he was moving in. Grayson had the staff paper spread across the desk, sixteen empty bars ruled off in pencil, and he'd been staring at them long enough that the lines had started to swim.

"Play me the thing," Quintin said, already picking out something loose on the low strings.

"It's not a thing yet. That's the problem. Mr. Chan says it's due Friday, chord changes and all, in real notation. I've got a melody but it just floats there. It doesn't land anywhere."

Quintin played the melody back from memory after one hearing, which was irritating, then played it again over a G chord, then an F, then back to G, letting each one ring until it went torpid and dull. "Better with something under it."

"That's what I can't figure out. Which somethings."

Quintin shrugged and reached for the chips. He had learned exactly three chords over two years of owning a guitar, and he built everything he played out of them, the same way a kid builds every structure out of the same three blocks. He didn't think of this as a limitation. He thought of it as a style. "I do C, F and G. All night if I have to. Works for every song I know."

Grayson wrote the letters at the top of the page and looked at them for a long moment. C was the first note of the scale, the one everything in the key of C leaned on. F was the fourth. G was the fifth. He counted it out on his fingers, not trusting himself, then counted again. Every song Quintin knew, and probably half the songs on the radio, built their chords on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the key. In C major that was C, F and G. It was so simple it felt like cheating.

"Those are the primary chords," he said. "Of a major key. The ones on one, four and five."

"Fancy," Quintin said, mouth full.

Grayson started placing the letters under his bars. C for the opening phrase, where the melody sat comfortably. F under the fifth bar, and the melody note that had seemed wrong all afternoon suddenly sounded deliberate, like it had been reaching for that change the whole time. He penciled in G at bar nine, crossed it out, moved it to bar ten, and the tune swung upward the way he'd wanted it to.

That was the evening Sebastian called. Grayson put the phone on the desk, propped against the lamp, and kept writing while Sebastian explained, at length, why melody writing was a matter of logos, of pure structure and reason, why the best composers derived their lines from intervals the way a proof derives its conclusions. Sebastian had taken one semester of theory enrichment and now contextualized everything, songs, arguments, cafeteria lunches, within systems he could diagram.

"Then explain why it sounds better over F," Grayson said.

"Sounds is not an argument."

"It's the only argument. It sounded flat for two days and it doesn't now."

Sebastian made a noise of deep skepticism and hung up somewhere in the middle of Grayson's next sentence. Grayson sat back. Part of him wanted Sebastian to be right, wanted a rule he could follow from here to the end, a logic that guaranteed the last six bars. But the three chords weren't a proof. They were more like a room he'd been handed, and the melody still had to find its own way to the walls.

He worked through dinner, which his mother brought up on a tray without comment, and past the hour when Quintin left, guitar case bumping the doorframe. Somewhere past ten he hit bar thirteen and stopped. F sounded right there but too safe, like the melody was deciding to go home early. G sounded restless in a way he liked but couldn't justify. He played both versions on the small keyboard, then a third that used neither, then the first one again. He wrote F, played it once, and left it, holding the pencil over the staff.

From the hallway, past midnight, his father saw the light still on and the boy bent over the paper, and he stood there a while without knocking, listening to the same six notes played three different ways, over and over, as if Grayson were asking each version a question and refusing to accept the first answer. The last six bars were still blank. Grayson played the phrase once more, wrote a single letter under bar fourteen, and then sat very still, listening to how it faded.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
The community kitchen on Alder Street opened at four, and by quarter past, Jonathan had claimed the burner by the window. He had the pot, the bag of onions Ms. Saleh had set aside for him, and forty minutes before his mother got off the bus. Soup for four, from almost nothing. That was the deal he'd made with himself on the walk over: if he could feed the family tonight, the money for the electric bill could stay where it was.

His sister had insisted on coming. She sat on the counter beside the sinks, swinging her heels against the cabinet, eleven years old and furious about something she wouldn't name. She peeled the papery skins off the onions while he cut, and Keely, who worked the Tuesday shift washing dishes, drifted over whenever the sink emptied.

"You're crying," Jonathan said, when her eyes went glassy over the cutting board.

"I'm not."

"You literally are."

"I'm not crying." She wiped her face with her sleeve, hard, and he almost let it go. Almost. He was about to tease her properly when she turned on him with real anger, the kind that had been waiting all afternoon for a place to land.

"It's not crying," she said. "It's the stupid onions. Ask him." She pointed at Ulysse, who had come in for the leftovers line and was standing near the door with his backpack still on.

Ulysse shrugged. "It's true. My uncle told me. Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes, and they produce this stuff, syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It's a vapor that irritates your eyes and makes them tear."

"Say that again," Jonathan said.

"Why?"

"Slower." He was already reaching for his phone to write it down, though he didn't know yet who he'd tell. His chemistry teacher had offered extra credit for anything from the real world, and the words had the shape of something a textbook would pay for: cells, enzymes, a compound with a name like a spell.

So it wasn't crying at all. Jonathan went back to the knife and found the thought wouldn't settle. It was chemistry, sure, and chemistry was on his side tonight, because he had learned at some point to keep the onions in the fridge, and cold ones released less of the vapor, or at least he'd always believed they did. Ms. Saleh had told him that years ago, back when he first started coming here. But now he wondered whether that was another of her half-true kitchen stories, the florid kind she told while stirring, the ones that made cooking sound like folklore. He could test it. There were two onions left, one cold from the walk over, one from the shelf.

He set his sister in front of the cold one and took the room-temperature one himself. "Cut," he said. "We'll see who tears up first."

"This is a dumb experiment."

"You're a dumb experiment."

She cut. He cut. Keely watched from the sink with her rubber gloves dripping, pretending not to be interested, and Ulysse drifted closer, which was as close as Ulysse ever got to enthusiasm.

Jonathan's eyes went first. He kept cutting anyway, refusing to admit it, until the tears ran and his sister pointed at him and laughed in a way that broke open the anger she'd carried in all afternoon. "You're crying," she said.

"It's the syn-propanethial-S-oxide," he said, and she laughed harder at the sound of it, and he laughed too, wiping his eyes with the back of his wrist. The cold-onion thing was wrong, then, or at least it had failed today, and he wrote that down too, because a finding that didn't work still counted for something. Maybe. He wasn't sure how to hold both ideas, the folklore and the chemistry, except to keep testing them against each other and stay honest about which ones survived.

The soup came together fast after that: stock from the bones Ms. Saleh kept in the freezer for him, the onions sweetened in the bottom of the pot, potatoes, the end of a bag of carrots. His sister tasted it and pronounced it "fine," which from her was a florid speech of praise. He ladled it into the two containers he'd brought, and then a third, because Keely always pretended she wasn't hungry and always ate.

Ms. Saleh came by at closing with her keys in her hand. "Same time Thursday?"

"Same time Thursday," Jonathan said. He thought about telling her the fridge thing hadn't worked, that her advice was a kind of artifice, well-meant, harmless, but unproven. Instead he said, "The cold onions didn't help. I checked."

"Good," she said. "Checking is the part that matters." She said it while locking the cabinet, not looking at him, and he couldn't tell whether it was wisdom or a habit of saying things that sounded like it.

Outside, his sister took one container and he took the other two, and they walked toward the bus stop where their mother would be getting off in nine minutes. His eyes still stung faintly. "It's not crying," his sister said, without being asked. "I know," he said. "I know."
